summary.name: Don't follow the sun.
summary.one_liner: An opinion essay by Will Larson arguing that "follow the sun" on-call rotations (splitting pages across time-zone shifts) are an ineffective approach to engineering on-call.
use_cases: Evaluating whether to split on-call across time zones
Deciding how to structure on-call tiers for exceptions versus routine service work
Making the case against offloading on-call to a separate reliability team
Reducing on-call stress and shift-handoff errors
Planning automation and game days to reduce human incident remediation
summary.what_it_does: The essay argues against "follow the sun" on-call, where a team's pages are split into multiple shifts across time zones, such as two 12-hour or three 8-hour shifts. It lists common motivations for adopting it (faster remediation, offloading on-call to a reliability team, reducing stress) and says the model appears to solve these without delivering long-term. The author lays out several objections: separate exception handling from service provision with distinct run and exception tiers, push remediation upstream into automation, game days, and architecture because humans are too slow, and recognize that more frequent shift transitions raise error rates. It also covers missing context for responders and the organizational problems of separating operations and product teams. The author notes that using on-call to deliver customer service across time zones can be a legitimate use.
notable: Written from the author's experience running a follow-the-sun on-call rotation at Uber for several years
Argues that exception handling and routine service work should be split into separate on-call tiers
Quantifies handoff impact: moving from one weekly shift to follow-the-sun yields fourteen shifts per week
Cited in dastergon/awesome-sre under Service Level Agreement
caveats: Opinion piece; the author's recommendations are not backed by a formal study beyond analogies to medical shift transitions and personal experience
Explicitly notes that follow-the-sun can be a legitimate choice when used to deliver customer service across time zones
